1044.title: What the long story teaches
1044.hook: faith kept through exile, loss and renewal
1044.howItsDone: In the Ardas, said standing at the close of Sikh services and at other moments, the sangat remembers the Gurus and the Sikhs who gave their lives for their faith, and ends by asking for chardi kala through the Name and the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pangat, and your line was tens of thousands fed. Today, a step back from the kitchen to look at the whole year's road.

Stand at the end of a long road and look back, and you can't see every step. You see the shape. A man with a musician beside him, walking from village to village. Towns built around a pool and a kitchen. Gurus who gave their lives rather than give way. A morning when five stood up. Hard years in the hills and forests. A kingdom won and lost. Marches with no weapons. A land split in two. A temple attacked, and grief in the streets. Families scattered across oceans, building gurdwaras in rented halls.
screen: `A MAN AND A MUSICIAN, WALKING.` → `MARTYRS, MARCHES, A LAND SPLIT.` → `GURDWARAS IN RENTED HALLS.`

segments.voice: The losses are real, and this story doesn't pretend. There were Gurus tortured and killed, families driven from their homes, sacred places damaged, and friends who never came back. Sikhs say those names out loud. In the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh services, the sangat recalls those who gave their lives and kept their faith: who were cut limb from limb, broken on wheels, sawn apart, and who kept their Sikhi with their uncut hair to the last breath. The losses are carried, standing, every day. And after every hard chapter, something kept going. The Granth kept being read. The kitchen kept cooking. The gurdwara door kept opening, in a village in Punjab, a river town in Malaysia, a rented hall in a northern winter. Sikhs often tell it this way: the faith didn't go on by winning every fight, but by keeping its daily practices. The Ardas ends with this line: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Through the Name, rising spirits, and by your will, the good of all. Chardi kala is the word for that spirit: rising, steady, even in loss. And notice what it asks for at the very end. Not victory. The good of all. As the Ardas holds it: remember everything, keep the practice, and keep asking good for everyone.
screen: `THE LOSSES ARE REAL.` · `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THEM.` · `THE KITCHEN KEPT COOKING.` · `CHARDI KALA, AND THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `THE LESSON OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Let the year's stories pass in front of you like a slow train, the musician, the five, the marches, the kitchens, without holding on to any of them. Let one stop, the one that stayed with you most, and as you breathe out, name quietly one thing it taught you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Chardi kala. Rising spirits, the steady, hopeful spirit asked for through the Name, kept through a faith's exile, loss and renewal. Today's word.
Your line: the lesson of the story. One lesson, named, is plenty. That's day one thousand forty-four.

1045.title: Your family's story
1045.hook: every Sikh family carries part of this history
1045.howItsDone: Sikh families pass on the sakhis of the Gurus and their own histories by telling them aloud, and some families and Sikh groups record elders' memories of migration, partition and community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala, and your line was the lesson of the story. Today the long story comes home, to an older voice and one question.

Where were you when you were my age? A boy asks it in the car on the way home from the gurdwara, mostly to fill the quiet. His grandfather, in the passenger seat, doesn't answer right away. Then he says the name of a village the boy has never heard. A well at the edge of it. A school two fields away. A morning when everyone packed what they could carry. The car pulls into the driveway, the engine stops, and nobody reaches for the door.
screen: `WHERE WERE YOU AT MY AGE?` → `A VILLAGE HE'S NEVER HEARD OF.` → `NOBODY REACHES FOR THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The big story lives in small ones. This year the path followed Gurus, marches, borders and ships, but the history doesn't sit only in books. Sikh families carry pieces of it: who crossed which border, who left a village, who drove a taxi through a first winter, who kept the Granth safe in a spare room. A family story is the long story at the size of one table. Sikhs pass on the Gurus' own lives as sakhis, stories told aloud, often by elders to children. The family story belongs to that same habit: the past handed over by voice. In the Japji, at the opening Angs of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak gives a run of short verses to suniai, listening. Each says what listening does: through listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away, and the devotees bloom. In Sikh practice, listening isn't only being polite. It's spiritual work. And how to ask? Some memories are sweet, and some hurt. A grandparent may laugh about a first job and go quiet about a border. So ask gently, one thing at a time, and let them decide how far to go. If they say no, that's an answer too. If they say yes, write it down, or ask to record it, because a story that lives in one voice can be lost. Elders are the archive no one else has.

segments.voice: Bring to mind an elder, a grandparent, a parent, an old neighbor, a teacher, someone at the gurdwara or a place of worship you know, and picture their hands. Breathe in and wonder what those hands have done that you've never heard about; breathe out and let one question form, the one you'd most like to ask, and just find it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

Your line: ask your elders. The car is still sitting in the driveway. Until tomorrow.

1046.title: Your place in the story
1046.hook: the story isn't over; you are part of what comes next
1046.howItsDone: Sikhs describe the daily life of a Sikh using passages such as Ang 305, where Guru Ram Das describes rising early, bathing and remembering the Name through the day, and they understand the Guru Granth Sahib and the Khalsa Panth as carrying the Gurus' work forward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sakhi, and your line was ask your elders. Today, the last page of this part of the long story, and the blank one after it.

A notebook, written almost to the end. The last lines are crowded: a kitchen on a highway, a turban explained at a table on a lawn, a river cleaned by hand, a forest on a scrap of dirt, a grandfather's story in a parked car. Then a page with nothing on it. Not torn out. Just waiting. That's where this part of the path has come, through the twentieth century and into today. The pen is on the table. Whose hand picks it up?
screen: `A NOTEBOOK, NEARLY FULL.` → `THE CROWDED LAST LINES.` → `A BLANK PAGE, WAITING.`

segments.voice: These last weeks weren't about the past. They were about Sikhs right now: in parliaments and at protests, in kitchens and classrooms, cleaning rivers, planting trees, arguing honestly about caste and about who may sing kirtan. Sikhs hold that the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru and the Khalsa Panth carries the work on, so the story keeps being written by ordinary people. What does an ordinary day look like? At Ang 305, Guru Ram Das describes the one who calls himself a Sikh of the True Guru: rising early, bathing, remembering the Name, and keeping it through the day, sitting or standing, with every breath and every bite. Nothing in that list is grand. It's a day, done with attention. Then the surprise. The same hymn closes with Guru Ram Das, a Guru, asking for the dust of the feet of that kind of Sikh: the one who remembers the Name and helps others remember it too. The Guru bows to the ordinary day. Whether you're Sikh, learning about Sikhs, or here for someone you love, the story goes on through small acts. A plate washed. A question asked. A neighbor's turban understood. A promise kept.
screen: `SIKHS RIGHT NOW, NOT ONLY THEN.` · `ANG 305: AN ORDINARY DAY.` · `THE GURU ASKS FOR THE DUST.` · `SMALL ACTS CARRY IT ON.` · then, large: `THE STORY GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Picture that notebook open to the empty page, and as you breathe in, ask what one thing today would be worth telling someone, years from now: not a big thing, something true. Breathe out, let one answer arrive, and see it on the page in your own handwriting, without judging it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

1047.title: Saka Nankana day
1047.hook: each February Sikhs remember the martyrs of Nankana, 1921
1047.howItsDone: On the yearly remembrance of Saka Nankana Sahib, gurdwaras hold kirtan and the Ardas in memory of the reformers, and pilgrims gather at Nankana Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gursikh, and your line was the story goes on. Now the path turns to the days Sikhs keep on the calendar, so the story is never lost.

Not every day on the Sikh calendar is a birthday or a harvest fair. Some are kept for grief. One of them belongs to Nankana Sahib, the town tradition holds as Guru Nanak's birthplace. On a morning in the last century, reformers came to its gurdwara to pray, and were killed there without lifting a hand. This path has already walked through that morning. Sikhs still keep it on the calendar, and today's practice asks for something small: one lamp.
screen: `NOT A BIRTHDAY, NOT A FAIR.` → `A MORNING AT NANKANA.` → `ONE LAMP.`

segments.voice: This begins a new stretch of the path: the calendar of memory. How a people keeps grief says a lot about them. Sikhs call a remembered episode of martyrdom like this a saka. Saka Nankana is that morning, and it remembers the reformers who walked into the gurdwara at Nankana Sahib, sat before the Guru Granth Sahib, and were attacked inside. These were not soldiers. Accounts say they had pledged not to strike back, and they kept the pledge. So the day doesn't remember a battle. It remembers a refusal: to answer violence with violence, even at the cost of their lives. It's kept with kirtan, and with the Ardas, the standing prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, which remembers those who gave their lives in service of the gurdwaras. Pilgrims gather at Nankana Sahib itself. Why kept this way? The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib on Ang 1, names the One as nirbhau and nirvair: without fear, without enmity. In the telling Sikhs keep, the reformers walked in without fear, and did not answer with enmity. So the day isn't kept with speeches against anyone. It's kept with a hymn and a prayer.
screen: `A CALENDAR OF MEMORY BEGINS.` · `A SAKA: A REMEMBERED MARTYRDOM.` · `KIRTAN, THE ARDAS, A LAMP.` · `WITHOUT FEAR, WITHOUT ENMITY.` · then, large: `THE PEACEFUL MARTYRS.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or small lamp and it's safe, light it and set it where you can see it; if not, rest your eyes on any small light near you, a screen dimmed low, a window. Let the flame stand for people who came to pray and did not strike back, and breathe slowly with two words to rest on: without fear, without enmity. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

1048.title: Saragarhi Day
1048.hook: every 12 September the twenty-one are remembered
1048.howItsDone: On Saragarhi Day, the Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army and Sikh gatherings elsewhere remember the soldiers of Saragarhi, often by reading their names, with Ardas and a moment of silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saka, and your line was the peaceful martyrs. Today's day of memory is about soldiers, and it's kept in a very different way.

The little post at Saragarhi talked to the world with a mirror and the sun: flashes of light sent from fort to fort across the ridge. Earlier on this path you heard how the signals kept coming the day the post was surrounded, and how the men inside stayed. Now the post is gone. What's left is a day on the calendar. On Saragarhi Day, in regimental halls, in gurdwaras and in homes, someone reads out a list of names, and people stand still while it's read.
screen: `A MIRROR AND THE SUN.` → `THE POST IS GONE.` → `A LIST OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: The story in one breath: Sikh soldiers of a British Indian regiment held a small signal post called Saragarhi, under Havildar Ishar Singh. A much larger force surrounded it. They held on, Sikh memory says, until the last of them had fallen. That memory counts them: twenty-one. The day is kept by name. The Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army marks Saragarhi Day, and so do Sikh gatherings far beyond it. A roll is read. Havildar Ishar Singh. The signaler, Gurmukh Singh. And the rest, one at a time. A number like twenty-one is easy to say and easy to forget. Names are harder to forget. Each name is a person who stayed. Sikhs often bring a verse to days like this. In a salok of Bhagat Kabir on Ang 1105, Kabir says, in paraphrase, that the true hero is the one who fights for the helpless, and who, though cut to pieces, never leaves the field. Some Sikh teachers read Kabir first as speaking of the inner battle, with one's own fear and greed. But his picture of someone who won't leave the field is why the salok is heard on a day like this. And the honest part: the men who attacked the post were fighting for their own valleys and homes. The day isn't kept against them. It's kept for twenty-one people, and for the plain fact that they stayed.
screen: `A SMALL POST, AND THEY STAYED.` · `THE DAY IS KEPT BY NAME.` · `KABIR: HE NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · `NOT KEPT AGAINST ANYONE.` · then, large: `TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand, feet planted, hands at your sides, and count slowly in your head to twenty-one, letting each count be one person; you don't need to know their names. Then sit down and let the breath steady itself. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them; if you don't, let the stillness be your way of honoring them.

1049.title: The thirteenth of April
1049.howItsDone: On Vaisakhi, people visit the Jallianwala Bagh memorial in Amritsar to remember those killed there, while the city also celebrates the harvest and the birth of the Khalsa. Some gurdwaras include the memory of the garden in their Vaisakhi gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saragarhi Day, and your line was twenty-one. Today, a day of memory that shares its date with a festival.

How do you keep a festival and a funeral on the same day? In Amritsar, that isn't a riddle. It's the calendar. In the morning, the city fills for Vaisakhi: the harvest is in, the Khalsa's birthday is sung, there's langar and color and noise. And a short walk from the Harmandir Sahib there's a walled garden where, on a Vaisakhi long ago, troops fired into an unarmed crowd. People come to that garden on the same day, quietly.
screen: `A FESTIVAL AND A FUNERAL?` → `VAISAKHI IN AMRITSAR.` → `A WALLED GARDEN.`

segments.voice: This path has told the story of Jallianwala Bagh, and the long memory of Udham Singh. Today is about what the date now carries. The firing happened on Vaisakhi day, so ever since, Vaisakhi in Punjab has held a second memory inside the first. Some celebrate in the morning and remember in the afternoon, and the two sit side by side. The crowd in the garden was Sikh, Hindu and Muslim together, some of them visitors in town for the festival. So the memory doesn't belong to one community, and people of different faiths come to the garden to remember. The garden is a memorial now. Visitors see the marks in the walls and the well, and some lower their voices without being told. A place can teach silence on its own. A line in the Guru Granth Sahib fits a mixed crowd. On Ang 1299, Guru Arjan sings, in paraphrase, that no one is my enemy and no one is a stranger; I get along with all. Some Sikhs hold that line beside the garden, because the people who died there were strangers to each other and are remembered together. It's also a guard against the easy road from grief to hatred: remembering the garden doesn't mean making enemies of anyone living today. So the festival isn't spoiled by the memory, and the memory isn't drowned by the festival.
screen: `ONE DATE, TWO MEMORIES.` · `A CROWD OF SEVERAL FAITHS.` · `THE GARDEN TEACHES SILENCE.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY.` · then, large: `VAISAKHI REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Sit, or stand if you'd rather, and for one minute say nothing and do nothing, no phone, no plans, letting the silence be for the people in the garden, Sikh, Hindu and Muslim, visitors and neighbors, who came for a festival. There's no need to picture what happened; when the minute feels done, breathe slowly and rest in the quiet a little longer. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.
Jallianwala Bagh. The walled garden in Amritsar where an unarmed crowd of several faiths was fired on, a memory the thirteenth of April, Vaisakhi, also holds. Today's word.
Your line: vaisakhi remembers. Joy and grief can share the same date. See you tomorrow.

1050.title: The great holocaust remembered
1050.hook: Sikhs gather at Kup Rahira to remember 1762
1050.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara with Ardas and kirtan in gurdwaras, and some gather at Kup Rahira, where the families were caught, to remember those who died there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jallianwala Bagh, and your line was vaisakhi remembers. Today, a day of memory with a hard name.

Flat fields, two villages, a road between them. On an ordinary day, the ground holds crops. But on the day of remembrance, cars and buses pull in, and Sikhs walk out across the fields toward a memorial at Kup Rahira: grandparents, parents, small children on shoulders. That's fitting, because what happened here happened to families. Sikhs call it the Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust. This path has told the day itself.
screen: `FLAT FIELDS, TWO VILLAGES.` → `FAMILIES WALK OUT TOGETHER.` → `THE VADDA GHALLUGHARA.`

segments.voice: A slow column of Sikh families, the old and the young, was caught in the open by Ahmad Shah Abdali's army. The fighters with them formed a ring and kept the column moving, fighting on the outside. The losses were terrible, and the old accounts don't agree on how many died. The remembrance doesn't turn on a figure. It turns on the people. You might expect a war memory to put soldiers in the middle. This one, in Sikh memory, puts the families there: the mothers, the children, the elders in the carts. The fighters are honored for one thing above all: they stayed between the danger and the ones who couldn't run. A hymn draws the same shape. On Ang 819, Guru Arjan sings, in paraphrase, that the hot wind does not touch the one under the Lord's shelter, and that all around is drawn the Lord's protecting circle, so pain cannot come near. The hymn is about the shelter of the Name, not a battle. But a circle drawn around the vulnerable is the same picture the accounts of that day leave. This week looked at chardi kala, sakhi, and your place in the story. Then the calendar of memory began: reformers who did not strike back at Nankana, twenty-one names at Saragarhi, a garden at Vaisakhi, and now this field. Each is kept with prayer and names, not with hatred for anyone living.
screen: `A COLUMN CAUGHT IN THE OPEN.` · `THE FAMILIES AT THE CENTER.` · `A PROTECTING CIRCLE, ANG 819.` · `A WEEK OF DAYS OF MEMORY.` · then, large: `THEY SHIELDED THE FAMILIES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one family you know, your own, a neighbor's, a friend's, then let the circle widen to families anywhere who are on the move, in danger, or simply worn out, and keep them inside it for a while without trying to fix anything. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them, or hold the line from Ang 819 in your heart. If you don't, simply wish them shelter.
Vadda Ghallughara. The great holocaust, the day Sikhs gather at Kup Rahira for the families caught in the open, and for those who formed a ring around them. Today's word.
Your line: they shielded the families. The circle was drawn around the ones who couldn't run. Day one thousand fifty, done.
